A vigil is a period of staying awake — usually through the night or for a long stretch of time — to watch over someone or something, to wait for something, or to honour someone, often in a serious or solemn situation.

Think of it this way: normally, night-time is for sleeping. A vigil is when someone deliberately refuses to sleep during that time, because something or someone demands their full, devoted attention.
The Three Elements That Define a Vigil

Almost every use of the word "vigil" contains these three qualities:

  1. Wakefulness — You are awake when you'd normally be asleep, or alert for a long, sustained period.
  2. Purpose — You aren't just randomly awake. You're awake for a reason — to watch, to wait, to pray, to honour, or to protect.
  3. Seriousness — A vigil is never casual. The word always carries a sense of weight, care, devotion, or solemnity. Nobody keeps a vigil over a pizza.
The Different Situations Where "Vigil" Is Used

The word appears in several different real-life contexts. Understanding each one will cement the meaning deeply.

1. A Vigil at a Sickbed or Deathbed

This is perhaps the most personal and emotionally raw use of the word. When someone is critically ill or dying, their loved ones may stay awake by their side through the night — holding their hand, watching over them, making sure they are not alone.

"The children kept a vigil at their father's bedside, not leaving the hospital for three days."

Here, the vigil is an act of love and loyalty. It says: "I will not sleep while you need me."

2. A Public or Candlelight Vigil

When a tragedy strikes a community — a mass shooting, a terrorist attack, the death of a beloved public figure — people often gather together in a public place, typically holding candles, to mourn collectively and show solidarity.

"Thousands of people attended a candlelight vigil in the city square to honour the victims of the attack."

This kind of vigil is about shared grief and respect. It is visible, communal, and symbolic. The candles represent light in darkness — both literally and emotionally.

3. A Religious Vigil

In many religious traditions, a vigil is a night spent in prayer, worship, or fasting — staying awake to focus spiritually on something sacred. For example, in Christianity, the "Easter Vigil" is a service held on the night before Easter Sunday, waiting and praying in anticipation of the resurrection. Monks in some traditions wake in the very early hours to pray as part of their daily discipline.

"The monks rose at 3 a.m. to observe their nightly vigil of prayer and scripture."

Here, the vigil is an act of devotion — choosing the discomfort of sleeplessness as a form of worship or spiritual discipline.

4. A Vigil of Waiting or Watching

Sometimes a vigil simply describes someone anxiously keeping watch and waiting for news or an outcome, without sleeping or resting.

"She kept a vigil by the window all night, waiting for her son to come home."
"The coast guard maintained a vigil over the stormy waters, watching for the missing vessel."

Here the meaning leans into the "watchfulness" side — staying alert, not letting your guard or attention drop.

The word "vigil" pairs with a small number of verbs very naturally. These are the phrases you'll most commonly see or hear:

  • Keep a vigil — "His friends kept a vigil outside the courtroom." (The most common phrase.)
  • Hold a vigil — "The community held a vigil for the missing child." (Used especially for public gatherings.)
  • Maintain a vigil — "Soldiers maintained a vigil at the border." (More formal, often implies ongoing watchfulness.)
  • A candlelight vigil — A public gathering where candles are held, usually in mourning or solidarity.
The Emotional Tone of the Word

This is important to understand, because it affects how and when you use the word. "Vigil" is never a light or cheerful word. It always carries one or more of these feelings:

  • Grief or mourning — honouring someone who has died or is suffering
  • Love and devotion — refusing to abandon someone even through the night
  • Anxiety and concern — waiting desperately for news
  • Reverence and spirituality — giving sacred time to something holy
  • Solidarity — standing together with others in difficult times

You would never say, "I kept a vigil waiting for the new video game to release." The word is too serious and weighty for trivial things.

• A watch can mean something similar, but it's more neutral and practical (like a security watch). A vigil has deeper emotional or spiritual weight.
  • A wake (in the funeral sense) is similar to a deathbed vigil, but a wake is specifically a gathering held after someone has died, often with people sitting with the body. A vigil can happen while someone is still alive, or in honour of someone not physically present.
  • Simply waiting has no built-in sense of devotion, solemnity, or sustained wakefulness. A vigil is a heightened, purposeful, serious form of waiting.

If you had to boil it all down: a vigil is a devoted, watchful, sleepless period of time kept out of love, grief, faith, or duty — the kind of waiting that says something matters too much to close your eyes.
